result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of the Athenian Acropolis. He tells of the lioness statue for Leæna, the arrow-pierced statue of Diitrephes and the Mycalessus massacre, a sailor's tale of Satyr islands, and further statues including the Wooden Horse and the figures of Thucydides and Phormio.

scenes.title: Tyrants and the lioness Leæna
scenes.summary: Pausanias compares Periander with the Pisistratidæ and tells how Hippias tortured Leæna to death. The Athenians later set up a bronze lioness and a statue of Aphrodite.
scenes.stakes: Leæna is tortured to death for the suspected knowledge of a plot.

scenes.title: Diitrephes and Mycalessus
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the statue of Diitrephes pierced by arrows and recalls his Thracians' massacre at Mycalessus. He then discusses the use of bows among the Greeks.
scenes.stakes: The people of Mycalessus are slaughtered by Thracian mercenaries.

scenes.title: Silenus's stone and the Satyr islands
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes statues of Hygiea and the stone of Silenus, then relays Euphemus's account of red-haired tailed Satyrs on distant islands.
scenes.stakes: Sailors are menaced by wild Satyrs and sacrifice a woman to save themselves.

scenes.title: More Acropolis statues and worthies
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists statues including Brauronian Artemis and the Wooden Horse, then tells of Thucydides's recall and Phormio's debts.
scenes.stakes: Thucydides is murdered after returning from exile; Phormio is burdened by debt.

alias_notes.explanation: Athene was worshipped under the title Hygiea, 'Health'.
Named for Brauron; the ancient statue there is called Tauric Artemis.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias gives the Athenian tradition of Leæna's torture, which he says no earlier history recorded.

analysis.text: Pausanias turns statues into occasions for history and digression, linking monuments to memory, cruelty and civic honour.
The Leæna story reflects Athenian tradition about the fall of the Pisistratid tyranny, and the Mycalessus massacre recalls the Peloponnesian War (413 BC).

fun_facts.text: Pausanias's account of the Mycalessus massacre in 413 BC agrees with Thucydides, who describes the Thracians slaughtering even schoolchildren.

language_notes.text: "The Lesbian tyrant" is Pittacus of Mytilene, usually counted among the Seven Wise Men; the sentence oddly treats Periander as another of the seven.
"Brazen" means made of bronze; "votive offering" is a gift dedicated to a deity.
Refers to the Athenian expedition to Sicily in 413 BC; Demosthenes had sailed with reinforcements, so the Thracians were sent home.
Homer's Catalogue of Ships in the Iliad describes the Locrians as fighting with bows and slings rather than spears and shields.
Philoctetes, from Malis, owned the bow of Heracles and fought at Troy. His fame explains the Malienses' archery.
Hygiea, goddess of health, was worshipped as Æsculapius's daughter; Athene took the same title, Athene Hygiea, as healer of the Athenians.
Carians came from southwest Asia Minor; Euphemus offers himself as an eyewitness source, a traveller's tale Pausanias reports.
"Handle" is a euphemism for sexual molestation; the next sentence confirms the assault.
Brauron, in Attica, had a famous sanctuary of Artemis; the Tauric Artemis image was said to be brought from the Taurians.
"Fatuous" means foolish; Pausanias argues the Wooden Horse was really a siege engine, since only fools would take it for a hollow wooden horse.
Thucydides is the historian of the Peloponnesian War, exiled from Athens; Œnobius's decree let him return.

context_notes.text: Hipparchus was killed in 514 BC by Harmodius and Aristogiton. Hippias, his brother, then ruled as a harsher tyrant until expelled in 510 BC.
Calamis was a famous fifth-century BC sculptor. The Athenians honored Leæna with a lioness, a pun on her name, rather than a human figure.
In 413 BC Thracian mercenaries sacked Mycalessus and killed many inhabitants, including schoolchildren, an atrocity recorded by Thucydides.
Satyrs were woodland spirits of Dionysus's retinue, part man and part horse or goat; Silenus was their aged leader and Dionysus's tutor.
Myron was a famed Athenian sculptor of the fifth century BC, best known for the Discus Thrower; Lycius was his son.
Phormio was a celebrated Athenian admiral of the Peloponnesian War; a township (deme) was a local district of Attica.

literary_notes.text: The bronze lioness commemorates Leæna by her name, a visual pun, and stands for her courage in staying silent under torture.
Pausanias interrupts the story with a traveler's curiosity, treating the arrows as an antiquarian puzzle that leads into a digression on archery.
Pausanias presents himself as a curious investigator who questions many informants, lending his digressions an air of personal inquiry.
Pausanias declines to describe the assault, letting reticence imply the horror.
The Athenians pay the debts of a noble admiral because they want him, reversing his reasoning that debt would undermine his authority.
